mathprize-olympiad-2011-01.title: Alternating sum
mathprize-olympiad-2011-01.body:
Let $E=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}A_{2i}-\frac12\sum_{i=0}^nA_i$. The even-indexed terms count with coefficient $1-\frac12=\frac12$ and the odd-indexed ones with $-\frac12$, so
$$E=\tfrac12\,(A_0-A_1+A_2-A_3+\cdots\pm A_n).$$
Since the sequence is nondecreasing, $A_{2j}-A_{2j+1}\le0$ and $A_{2j+1}-A_{2j+2}\le0$.

**$n$ even.** Group as $2E=(A_0-A_1)+(A_2-A_3)+\dots+(A_{n-2}-A_{n-1})+A_n\le A_n$. Group instead as $2E=A_0+(A_2-A_1)+(A_4-A_3)+\dots+(A_n-A_{n-1})\ge A_0\ge0$. So $0\le E\le\frac{A_n}2$.

**$n$ odd.** Group as $2E=(A_0-A_1)+(A_2-A_3)+\dots+(A_{n-1}-A_n)\le0$. Group instead as $2E=A_0-A_n+(A_2-A_1)+\dots+(A_{n-1}-A_{n-2})\ge A_0-A_n\ge-A_n$. So $-\frac{A_n}2\le E\le0$.

In both cases $|E|\le\frac{A_n}2$. ∎

mathprize-olympiad-2011-02.title: Constant angle
mathprize-olympiad-2011-02.body:
Fix $r$ and write $D=D_r$, $E=E_r$, $P=P_r$. Since $ABC$ is equilateral, $AB=CA$ and $\angle ABE=\angle CAD=60^\circ$; also $BE=r\cdot BC=r\cdot AB=AD$. By SAS, $\triangle ABE\cong\triangle CAD$ (with $A\to C$, $B\to A$, $E\to D$). Hence $\angle BAE=\angle ACD$.

Let $x=\angle BAE=\angle ACD$ and $y=\angle EAC$ (so $x+y=\angle BAC=60^\circ$). In triangle $APC$ we have $\angle PAC=y$ and $\angle PCA=x$, hence
$$\angle APC=180^\circ-(x+y)=120^\circ.$$
This holds for every $r$. Moreover each $P_r$ lies inside the triangle, on the same side of line $AC$ as $B$.

The locus of points $X$ on that side of $AC$ with $\angle AXC=120^\circ$ is an arc of a single circle through $A$ and $C$ (inscribed angle theorem and its converse). Hence all $P_r$ lie on the circle through $A$, $C$ and $P_{1/2}$. ∎

mathprize-olympiad-2011-03.title: Pair up divisors
mathprize-olympiad-2011-03.body:
Since $24\mid n+1$, we have $n\equiv-1\pmod 8$ and $n\equiv-1\pmod3$; in particular $n\equiv3\pmod4$, so $n$ is not a perfect square (squares are $0$ or $1$ mod $4$). Hence the positive divisors of $n$ split into pairs $\{a,b\}$ with $a\ne b$, $ab=n$.

**Claim: $24\mid a+b$ for each pair.** We have $(a+1)(b+1)=ab+a+b+1=(n+1)+(a+b)$, and $24\mid n+1$, so it suffices to show $24\mid(a+1)(b+1)$, i.e. $3$ and $8$ both divide it.

- Mod $3$: $ab=n\equiv2\pmod 3$, so neither $a$ nor $b$ is divisible by $3$ and their residues are $1,2$ in some order; hence one of $a,b$ is $\equiv2$ and $3$ divides $a+1$ or $b+1$.
- Mod $8$: $ab\equiv3\pmod4$ forces $a,b$ odd with $\{a,b\}\equiv\{1,3\}\pmod4$. Then $a+1,b+1$ are $\equiv\{2,0\}\pmod 4$: one of them is divisible by $4$ and the other by $2$, so $8\mid(a+1)(b+1)$.

Therefore $24\mid(a+1)(b+1)$ and so $24\mid a+b$. Summing over all pairs, $24$ divides the sum of all divisors of $n$. ∎

mathprize-olympiad-2011-04.title: Weights and AM-GM
mathprize-olympiad-2011-04.body:
If $a=0$, every entry is $0$ and $r>10^c\ge10$, so there are at least two (identical) rows. Let $a>0$ and suppose, for contradiction, that all rows are distinct.

Put $p=\frac a{a+1}\in(0,1)$. Give a row $(x_1,\dots,x_c)$ the weight $p^{x_1+\dots+x_c}=\prod_j p^{x_j}$.

**Upper bound.** Expanding $(1+p+p^2+\cdots)^c$ gives the sum of the weights of *all* possible rows of $c$ nonnegative integers, each exactly once. Since the rows of $M$ are distinct, their total weight $W$ satisfies
$$W\le\left(\frac1{1-p}\right)^c=(a+1)^c.$$

**Lower bound.** Let $S_i$ be the sum of row $i$, so $\sum_iS_i=arc$ and $W=\sum_{i=1}^rp^{S_i}$. By AM-GM,
$$W\ge r\Bigl(\prod_i p^{S_i}\Bigr)^{1/r}=r\,p^{(\sum S_i)/r}=r\,p^{ac}.$$

**Compare.** From $rp^{ac}\le(a+1)^c$,
$$r\le\left(\frac{a+1}{a}\right)^{ac}(a+1)^c=\left[\left(1+\tfrac1a\right)^{a}(a+1)\right]^c.$$
Since $\ln(1+t)<t$ for $t>0$, we have $a\ln\left(1+\frac1a\right)<1$, i.e. $\left(1+\frac1a\right)^a<e<10$. Hence $r<(10a+10)^c$, contradicting $r>(10a+10)^c$. So two rows of $M$ are identical. ∎
